newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda's guilty and innocent together again.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda's guilty and innocent together again.

text.p: The innocent and the guilty from Rwanda's genocide stood shoulder to shoulder under a beating sun, together again nearly three years after playing their parts in one of the century's greatest slaughters.
They listened attentively to speeches by two government ministers and the deputy chief of the army who had come to Nyamata, the main town in Kanzenze commune, to explain what lay in store.
"You have come back, now help reconstruct your country," said Anastase Gasana, Rwanda's foreign minister and the leader of the delegation from the capital, Kigali, 40 km (25 miles) away.
"Those of you who committed genocide, you did something bad and you are going to be put on trial," he told the guilty ones, anonymous in the crowd of about 1,000 of Kanzenze commune's 64,000 people.

Before the mass killing in Rwanda began on April 6, 1994, the commune had a population of 120,000. Within weeks 50,000, almost exclusively from the minority Tutsi tribe, had been killed by machetes, clubs and, for the fortunate, bullets.

Some of the worst killing was done in the churches at Nyamata and Ntarama which have become internationally famous and are being converted into national monuments to the estimated 800,000 victims of the genocide.

Then Gasana delivered his message to the innocent, the Tutsis who survived the slaughter and decided to stay and the larger group of Tutsis who returned from decades of exile abroad after the three-month genocide was over and the hardline Hutu government which organised it had lost the civil war.
"Do not take the law into your own hands. The government will arrest the guilty. Do not make false denunciations," the minister warned at Thursday's meeting.
Rwanda began trials in late December under its Genocide Law. The first defendants under the law's category one, for the most guilty, have been sentenced to death by firing squad.
Government delegations delivered similar messages of justice and reconciliation throughout the traumatised country this week.

The visits were needed because of the sudden repatriation of more than one million Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled in 1994 after their community committed the genocide and their government army was defeated by Tutsi rebels.

The refugees who have come back since last November had little choice in the matter because those in camps in Zaire were displaced by a rebellion there and those in Tanzania were effectively ordered to leave.

There has not been the vindictive and arbitrary round-up of genocide suspects which many feared. By the end of December, U.N. human rights monitors calculate 5,000 returnees, or 0.5 percent of the total, had been arrested.

"I am astonished in a positive way. The authorities and the local people, apart from a small number, have done their best to welcome the returnees," said Albert Colin, a 65-year-old Belgian Catholic priest at Nyamata.

"The drama that happened in Rwanda was unimaginable. Not a single Rwandan was untouched by it and those responsible must be tried," said Colin, a resident of the tiny central African country since 1974.

Commune officials in Kanzenze, consulting the immaculate statistics that have always been a feature of the former German and Belgian colony's administration, said 12,204 Hutu refugees had returned by January 12, increasing the commune's population by 23 percent.
Among those numbers is Valerie Mukamwezi, a Hutu who returned to Nyamata with her husband and four children last November 19 after 28 months in a refugee camp in Zaire.
"There is no problem with the people here," she said, clearly nervous about being interviewed by journalists.

Her husband had gone to the meeting addressed by Gasana. She stood outside their tent, on the tiny slice of land they owned before the genocide. They found their little house destroyed when they got back.
She said four of the Hutus who came back to Nyamata with her, three men and a woman, had been arrested so far.

In Kanzenze the killing rate was so high that many if not most of the commune's Hutus must have taken part. Some of the most guilty are certain to have stayed in Zaire, preferring to roam in misery and hunger rather than be arrested, tried and executed at home.
But there is no doubt that many of the 12,000 returnees are also guilty and fear arrest.
"Our first task was to repatriate the people," said the foreign minister, a Hutu in the bi-ethnic government.
"But justice will then be done, whether it is in one year's time or two or five or 10 or 20."
